I’d develop **paper theatre with constructivist composition** first. It offers a tactile, authored look and a natural Parallax signature: layers shift when the argument reveals a different perspective.

I generated five directions, plus a bolder risograph variation:

| Direction | My assessment |
|---|---|
| **Woodcut** | Strong, graphic, closest to your current identity. Needs less uniform texture. |
| **Paper theatre** | Best potential for a recognizable world, staged reveals, and controlled layer movement. |
| **Charcoal + spot color** | Most intimate and reflective. Strong alternative for philosophical storytelling. |
| **Gouache** | Warm and humane, though currently less differentiated. |
| **Graphic risograph** | Boldest departure. The blue/red variation has stronger shape and color identity; its figures need more personality. |

One useful discovery: the initial palette pulled several styles toward nostalgic sepia. **Our identity needs consistent composition, proportions, and selective detail alongside the medium.**

For animation, the research suggests three practical priorities:

- **Start with clean, readable anatomy and objects.** Runway warns that flaws in hands and faces can intensify in video; it recommends letting the image establish appearance while the prompt describes motion. [Runway guide](https://help.runwayml.com/hc/en-us/articles/48324313115155-Image-to-Video-Prompting-Guide).
- **Evaluate texture stability and completed movement separately.** Fine detail can flicker, while an almost frozen clip can appear very consistent. [VBench++](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.13503v1).
- **Use additional controls for ambitious shots.** First/end frames and camera motion references provide useful constraints; Adobe documents both. [Adobe guide](https://helpx.adobe.com/firefly/web/work-with-audio-and-video/work-with-video/match-camera-motion-to-reference-video.html).

My design inference is to favor clear silhouettes, separated hands, broad marks, and room for the action. **Featureless faces alone won’t solve difficult movement.** Paper gives us a controllable layer-animation route; its reliability for AI-generated body movement still needs testing.

I saved [all studies and the research brief](/Users/feihuyan/project-parallax/project/visual-identity/2026-10-10/README.md), plus the [exact generation prompts](/Users/feihuyan/project-parallax/project/visual-identity/2026-10-10/studies.json). The brief includes a comparison test covering quiet movement, a gesture, and a coin handoff.

**My shortlist: paper theatre, charcoal, and the bolder graphic print.**
Can you do more research on additional potential directions?

I found **eight additional directions worth considering**. The strongest new candidates are **modernist cel animation, conceptual line drawing, and architectural surrealism**. They offer different ways to tell a story, beyond changing the texture of the image.

These are artistic and production assessments; their performance in AI video still needs testing.

1. **Modernist cel animation — expressive, graphic, theatrical.**  
   Irregular ink contours, asymmetrical settings, selective color, and distinctive human poses. UPA provides a strong precedent for both comedy and serious drama. I’d prioritize this for human storytelling and larger gestures. [UPA at MoMA](https://www.moma.org/calendar/exhibitions/2434).

2. **Conceptual line drawing — intelligent, personal, quietly witty.**  
   A line can become a person, a wall, a boundary, or an explanation. This could suit philosophy particularly well: the drawing changes as the reasoning develops. Precise transformations would work well through authored animation. [Saul Steinberg references](https://saulsteinbergfoundation.org/essay/drawing-table-reliefs/).

3. **Architectural surrealism — mysterious, spacious, cerebral.**  
   Simplified rooms, long shadows, unexpected scale, and deliberately conflicting perspectives. A viewpoint change could reveal the relationship between two situations—a strong fit for Parallax. The challenge is giving every spatial oddity a purpose. [De Chirico at MoMA](https://www.moma.org/artists/1106-giorgio-de-chirico).

4. **Ink wash with crisp figures — atmospheric and humane.**  
   Broad washes and substantial empty space, with sharper detail around people and consequential objects. This could support water, weather, walking, and reflective scenes. I’d explore cool ink with a restrained colored accent. [Tyrus Wong’s concept paintings](https://www.waltdisney.org/blog/look-closer-concept-art-tyrus-wong).

5. **Drawn surreal collage — strange, analytical, layered.**  
   Carefully combined illustrated fragments and changes of scale could connect domestic situations with larger systems. It offers useful reveal mechanisms, though dense engraving could become visually busy. [Max Ernst’s collage novels](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/25930).

6. **Rotoscoped editorial drawing — observed movement, illustrated appearance.**  
   Establish a performance first, then translate it into economical contours and painted planes. This is worth exploring for ambitious body movement. The drawing needs deliberate simplification to avoid looking like filtered footage. [Flat Black Films’ work](https://flatblackfilms.com/Flat_Black_Films/Bob_Sabiston.html).

7. **Pinscreen-inspired tonal worlds — velvety, sculptural, dreamlike.**  
   Images emerge through soft relief and shadow. This feels promising for uncertainty, memory, and unsettling philosophical passages. I’d initially use it as an occasional register. [Watch *Mindscape* at NFB](https://www.nfb.ca/film/mindscape/).

8. **Paint-on-glass — fluid, intimate, continuously transforming.**  
   Painted forms can be revised into other images as an interpretation changes. It offers a compelling transition language, with recognizable anchors needed to keep transformations meaningful. [Caroline Leaf’s technique](https://collection.nfb.ca/film/the-art-of-the-animator-part-i).

A useful technical finding is that **ambitious movement can begin with a source performance and then be restyled**. Runway documents that workflow through Aleph. It deserves comparison with generating movement directly from a still. [Runway restyling guide](https://help.runwayml.com/hc/en-us/articles/52150503729171-Aleph-2-0-Prompting-Guide).

**My strongest new combination:** expressive ink-drawn people inside geometric, subtly impossible spaces, with perspective changes tied to changes in the argument. That could retain constructivism’s strength while developing a warmer, more individual identity.

What do you think so far?

**I see two strong candidates for the channel’s identity: architectural surrealism and paper theatre. Charcoal has the strongest human feeling.** We have useful ingredients, but I wouldn’t call any sample the finished Parallax look yet.

| Direction | What I like | What needs work |
|---|---|---|
| **8 — Architectural surrealism** | The space itself can express a philosophical idea. Changes of perspective could become a recognizable Parallax gesture. | The figures feel like mannequins, and the architecture feels borrowed from an established painting tradition. It needs more contemporary, particular human life. |
| **2 — Paper theatre** | The most coherent material world: people, objects and scenery belong together. Moving scenery could reveal context beautifully. | Currently too gentle and nostalgic. Sharper compositions, a less brown palette and more expressive silhouettes would give it character. |
| **3 — Charcoal** | The most intimate and observant. The clothing, posture and imperfect marks suggest someone actually looking at people. | The sepia treatment feels familiar. It needs stronger composition and more selective texture to become recognizable. |

**My biggest concern is that several samples still share the same underlying illustration, with a different surface treatment.** Realistically proportioned bodies, erased facial features and attractive texture can still produce a generic AI look. We need consistent decisions about the entire figure: proportions, gestures, hands, clothing and contours.

A few other honest reactions:

- **Conceptual line drawing:** I like its potential more than this execution. The current sample is a pleasant outline drawing; the line needs to do something intellectually surprising.
- **Risograph:** strong immediate color identity, but the people approach familiar editorial illustration.
- **Cel animation:** clearly differentiated, but this version feels too cheerful and retro for the tone you’ve described.
- **Collage:** the sample hasn’t yet delivered the unexpected relationships that make collage compelling.

My preferred direction remains **expressive ink-drawn people inside geometric, subtly impossible spaces**, with the same line vocabulary carrying explanations and diagrams. Keep constructivism’s compositional strength, and give the people more individuality and warmth.

I’d now develop that direction and paper theatre across three very different scenes: a human encounter, a physical rescue, and an abstract explanation. The bakery setting pulls almost everything toward nostalgia. Seeing those other scenes—and testing movement—will tell us much more than another round of medium names.

what do you think of these against our constructivist

Looking side by side, **our constructivist work is currently the stronger overall identity. The surrealist studies offer the stronger storytelling ideas.** I’d develop a combination of those strengths.

| Aspect | Current constructivist | New surrealist studies |
|---|---|---|
| Tone | Serious, contemplative, visually substantial | Warmer and more approachable, but sometimes too storybook |
| Recognition | Consistent palette, angular figures and strong tonal structure | The spatial ideas are distinctive; the drawing style feels more familiar |
| Human presence | Posture carries emotion, though faces can feel like masks | More expressive and particular people |
| Visual storytelling | Clearly establishes situations | Can reveal distance, interpretation and conflicting perspectives |

The existing **dinner and rescue images have more adult weight** than the latest shop illustrations. I wouldn’t lose that. The new rounded faces, gentle expressions and distressed blue surfaces pull us toward a familiar illustrated children’s book aesthetic.

But the constructivist images have their own weakness: **the repeated triangulation and dense texture across faces, clothing and surroundings can look algorithmic.** Their strongest qualities are the composition, silhouettes and controlled light—not necessarily all that surface detail.

For Parallax, I’d let constructivism define the shapes, contrast and composition, and let surrealism define how the world behaves:

- Keep the strong silhouettes and ink/bone/amber anchors.
- Make people less rigid through posture, hands and a few organic contours.
- Reduce uniform faceting and texture.
- Introduce one meaningful contradiction: shadows connect, a counter changes perspective, or a surface reveals another role.

**The shadow study is the most promising addition.** It communicates something the existing style doesn’t yet do, and it could work beautifully within the current visual language. The continuous-surface idea is another strong candidate.

The next useful comparison would be the **same shadow scene rendered in our constructivist style**. That would show whether we can gain surrealism’s expressive range while preserving the seriousness and coherence we already have.

What should we do next around our visual research

**I’d now research how this becomes a recognizable system across an episode.** We have a promising combination: faceted featureless people, selective painted detail and purposeful surrealism.

The next questions are:

1. **Can we draw the same person consistently?**  
   Make a reference sheet with front, three-quarter and side views, plus a few head angles. Keep the latest facial treatment. This will reveal which planes define the character and which should change with the light.

2. **Can the compositions become more distinctive?**  
   Our samples often use warm interiors, centered interactions and detailed backgrounds. Test stronger cropping, larger empty areas, groups of people and daylight scenes. Jacob Lawrence is a useful reference for expressive abstracted figures, staged spaces and continuity across a narrative series. [MoMA’s Migration Series overview](https://www.moma.org/calendar/exhibitions/444).

3. **How should the facets work throughout the image?**  
   Compare two treatments of the same scene: angular planes concentrated on the person, versus planes that connect person, architecture and light. Feininger’s overlapping prismatic planes offer a useful reference for that second experiment. My concern is that equally sharp facets everywhere could become visually repetitive. [Whitney’s Feininger overview](https://whitney.org/artists/417).

4. **What makes surrealism specifically Parallax?**  
   Develop three recurring operations: independent shadows, continuous surfaces and a changed viewpoint revealing a hidden relationship. For each, show a clear **before and after**, tied to an actual sentence from the script. The shadow study communicates its contradiction more clearly than the desk’s folded surface does.

**My recommended next deliverable:** one character reference sheet and a six-frame storyboard from the episode, including an ordinary human scene, a surreal reveal and an analytical graphic. That would let us assess consistency, storytelling and how the illustration sits beside our typography.

Motion testing should follow; its reliability remains unresolved because the video trials haven’t run.

My strongest recommendations:

- **Characters:** preserve the detailed, featureless heads; establish consistent proportions across angles and communicate emotion through posture.
- **Composition:** explore daylight, crowds, close crops and institutional spaces. [Jacob Lawrence](https://www.moma.org/interactives/exhibitions/2015/onewayticket/static/panel/10/) offers useful lessons in alternating density and quiet.
- **Facets:** connect selected planes across people, architecture and light. [Feininger](https://whitney.org/collection/works/386) is especially relevant.
- **Surrealism:** develop precise contradictions and changes of viewpoint that reveal context. [Magritte](https://www.nga.gov/artworks/70170-la-condition-humaine) provides a strong precedent.

**My preferred direction remains faceted people, selective painted detail, varied compositions and occasional spatial reveals.**

The guide includes a character-sheet experiment, three facet comparisons, three surreal experiments and a six-frame episode pilot. Animation suitability remains untested.

**Our prompting contributed, and my earlier assessment was too generous.** We polished an unresolved pose, then explicitly told the model to preserve it.

After reviewing the images, exact prompts and research, I see four problems:

- **We locked the defective grip.** The ending prompt called it “EXACT correctly drawn” and said “Do not redraw or simplify those hands.” That carried the same ambiguous anatomy into the next image.
- **Our reference solved only a small part of the scene.** It showed overlapping wrists, without shoulders, elbows or body weight. The generator still had to invent how two bodies connect around that grip.
- **We constrained connected parts separately.** We preserved forearms and contact positions while moving shoulders, elbows and knees. That left little freedom to reconstruct a convincing whole pose.
- **Detail disguised the structural problem.** Knuckle shading and finger marks made the hands look finished, but you still cannot easily trace each wrist into its own palm.

The research supports this distinction. **HandRefiner** identifies articulation and occlusion as major difficulties and reports trouble with complex intertwined fingers even with specialized geometry-based repair. That supports using stronger structural guidance; it does not establish the internal cause of our particular generator’s failure. [HandRefiner paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2311.17957v2)

Official OpenAI guidance recommends explicit reference roles, separating changes from preservation constraints, and refining one thing at a time. Our reference labels were reasonable; what we chose to preserve was wrong. Longer prompts alone are not an established fix. [Official image prompting guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/image-prompting)

**My recommendation is to change the workflow before another finished rebuild:**

1. Find or construct a believable **whole-body pulling pose**, with readable hand contact from the intended camera.
2. Generate a simple figure study with minimal scenery, allowing the linked arms and shoulders to change together.
3. Approve anatomy and weight first.
4. Apply our painted treatment and featureless heads, then check that the structure survives.

This follows the reference → pose blocking → polish approach used in animation practice. [Push-and-pull body mechanics](https://www.animationmentor.com/blog/tutorial-animating-pushing-and-pulling-motions/)

| **Painted object portraits** | A coin, loaf, cup, key or mechanical component treated as a carefully composed still life. Rich selected detail against a quiet field. [Morandi’s objects](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/761049) suggest how ordinary things can establish a distinctive vocabulary. | Move the object and its shadow separately; introduce a second object or change their arrangement. |
| **Cutaway and exploded objects** | A familiar object opens to reveal its structure: a machine, building, container or mechanism. Painted surfaces with precise diagrammatic edges. | Separate parts, reveal interiors and connect components in an exact sequence. Particularly promising for explanations. |
| **Drawn analytical overlays** | Thin ink contours, brackets, highlighted regions and translucent painted planes over a scene. The same picture can receive two different interpretations. | Draw connections, isolate a relationship, or switch the overlay while holding the underlying scene still. |
| **Painted backgrounds for graphics** | Bone paper, a broad plaster-like plane, an architectural shadow or a restrained ink wash at the edges. The chart or typography occupies a deliberately quiet area. | Reveal charts and text above the painting; move a shadow or foreground plane when it helps direct attention. |

**Overlays deserve their own experiment.** I’d compare two families:

- **Analytical:** drawn lines, boundaries, brackets and annotations that explain something.
- **Atmospheric:** window shadows, translucent washes and foreground silhouettes that establish space or mood.

We should judge each by what it adds to the picture. A consistent overlay vocabulary could become one of our strongest identifying features.

For Remotion, I’d design these as **separate background, object, shadow and foreground assets**, with labels and connections added in code. That gives us control over timing and movement. Remotion’s documentation also recommends loading images through its image component and driving animation from the frame timeline for reliable rendering. [Image handling](https://www.remotion.dev/docs/img), [animation guidance](https://www.remotion.dev/docs/flickering).

how can we combine some of these with our remotion? is there a natrula synergy there

**Yes—there’s a strong natural synergy.** Painted images can give Parallax its atmosphere and visual character; Remotion can add precise explanations, movement and timing.

The most interesting combination is **graphics that emerge from the illustration**. A scene can gradually become an explanation while keeping the viewer in the same visual world.

| Visual material | How we combine it with Remotion | Best use |
|---|---|---|
| Architectural scenery | Move toward a detail, then draw anchored contours and callouts | Introducing a situation, then explaining its structure |
| Transparent painted objects | Position, reveal and compare objects alongside diagrams or text | Making abstract ideas tangible |
| Surreal cutaways | Cut between an ordinary object and its impossible interior, then annotate it | Revealing hidden assumptions or alternative explanations |
| Quiet painted backgrounds | Place existing charts and diagrams over the clear central area | Keeping analytical sequences visually connected to the illustrations |
| Foreground overlays | Frame a scene or reveal it through an opening | Occasional transitions and changes of viewpoint |

Our code already has much of this: `ScrollyReveal` combines images, camera movement and annotations; `ImageComposite` handles image layouts; the episode system supports painted backdrops beneath graphics. Remotion’s frame-based animation gives us control over when each element appears relative to narration. [Remotion animation documentation](https://www.remotion.dev/docs/animating-properties).

For **AI care and motives**, I’d test a short sequence like this:

1. **An ordinary painted cup:** establish something familiar.
2. **Cut to its architectural interior:** introduce the metaphor of an unseen inner world.
3. **Draw annotations:** distinguish what we observe from what we infer.
4. **Move into a diagram on matching painted paper:** show different explanations for the same outward action.

The connection comes from carrying the object, colors and drawing language across those shots.

A few production choices would make this coherent: consistent line weights and typography, restrained movement, and preserving the paintings’ original colors. Some existing annotation templates automatically apply duotone treatment, so they need a small adjustment. True scenery parallax would also require separate foreground and background assets.

**I’d make that 20–30-second combined sequence next.** The eight individual studies demonstrate the ingredients; a continuous sequence would show whether they feel like one distinctive Parallax identity.
